quotes.text: Wernicke aphasia (WA) represents a fluent aphasia characterized by markedly impaired auditory–verbal comprehension with relatively preserved rate, prosody, and grammar but frequent semantic and phonemic paraphasias, neologisms, and jargon.
Carl Wernicke and Ludwig Lichtheim developed the classical model of aphasia in the 19th century, which was further refined neuroanatomically by Norman Geschwind in the 1960s.

This model provides the foundation for understanding the clinical features of aphasia and the corresponding neuroanatomical lesions.[1] According to this model, language processing begins with comprehension in the Wernicke area, located in the posterior section of the superior temporal gyrus, Brodmann area 22.
Information is then conveyed through the arcuate fasciculus to the Broca area in the inferior frontal gyrus, responsible for language output or expression.
[Figure] The Broca and Wernicke Areas of the Brain.
The Wernicke area is responsible for language comprehension, while the Broca area is responsible for language expression.

It is composed of approximately 200 million heavily myelinated nerve fibers that form homotopic or heterotopic projections to contralateral neurons in the same anatomical layer.[1] During infancy, the corpus callosum expands rapidly due to an increase in the number of axons, axon diameter, and myelin.

As the Latin translation of "cingulate" would suggest, the cingulate gyrus wraps around the corpus callosum like a "belt." It begins beneath the rostrum of the corpus callosum, curves around the genu, and projects above the superior surface of the body of the corpus callosum, reaching its posterior end where it terminates at the isthmus of the cingulate gyrus.
